newsitem.title: GERMANY: Two Turks surrender as Maltese plane hijack ends.
newsitem.headline: Two Turks surrender as Maltese plane hijack ends.

text.p: German police questioned two Turkish airline hijackers on Monday but said they learned nothing more about their bid to free a man who tried to kill the Pope.

The hijackers gave themselves up on Monday morning after a six-hour drama in which they threatened to blow up an Air Malta flight with 80 people aboard and forced it to fly to Cologne instead of Istanbul.
No one was hurt and the "explosives" strapped to the chest of one of the hijackers turned out to be a harmless fake.
Before surrendering they demanded the release of Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Agca, who is serving a life sentence in Italy for trying to assassinate Pope John Paul in 1981.
"The hijackers made no political demands, they just wanted to attract sympathy for the...assassin (Agca) in a television interview," Cologne police chief Juergen Roters told a news conference.

"We have no further information about the motives of the suspect," Cologne police said in a statement on Monday evening. "Based on the available information it appears that the two suspects did not have any further accomplices."

Authorities identified them as 25-year-old Ismail B. and 24-year-old Nosret A., who was wanted in Germany for failing to pay a 300 mark ($200) fine after a court found him guilty of shoplifting in Rostock.

German police had established contact with one of the men through a Turkish-speaking interpreter and persuaded him to hand over to the pilot what was supposed to be the fuse of their explosive device.
During negotiations, the hijackers requested an interview with a television crew in the presence of a human rights group, but before this could take place they gave themselves up.

Police officer Winrich Granitzka said about 30 minutes into the flight one of the man went into the cockpit and showed the pilot what looked like sticks of dynamite strapped to his chest. He then ordered the pilot to divert to plane to Germany.
The airliner landed at the busy Cologne-Bonn airport 15 km (10 km) south of the city of Cologne at 0247 GMT and stood at a freight section there.
Granitzka said the man eventually handed over a black piece of plastic said to be the fuse to the pilot and the two men surrendered. "The device turned out to be a fake," he said.

Prosecutors said the two men would be brought before a judge on Tuesday to be formally arrested on charges of a dangerous attack on air traffic. If convicted they could face between five and 15 years in jail.
Police earlier said 90 people were on the flight, including five crew and the two hijackers.

They later revised this figure to 80 including 74 passengers and six crew. Among the passengers were Turks, Libyans, Maltese, Russians, Tunisians and Germans. Some were to fly to Istanbul later on Monday and the rest were to leave on Tuesday.

The hijackers had let five of the passengers leave the plane shortly after landing. One of them was a woman with heart problems, who was treated on the spot. Two others were taken to hospital suffering shock.
The hijacking was the first involving an Air Malta aircraft and the first of a flight originating in Malta.
Maltese Prime Minister Afred Sant announced an inquiry into security for the flight and Malta sent a magistrate to Germany to join investigations.
